before.content_html:
What Was the Wall Street Crash?

The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 was the sudden collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange. In days, billions of dollars were wiped out, ruining millions of investors and triggering the worst economic depression in modern history.

The mood before the Crash was one of total confidence. During the 1928 presidential campaign, Republican candidate Herbert Hoover promised Americans “a chicken in every pot and two cars in every garage.” This summed up the overconfidence of the era — the belief that prosperity would last forever.

Long-Term Causes of the Crash

The Crash did not happen overnight. Serious weaknesses had been building throughout the 1920s:

Speculation

Millions of ordinary Americans bought shares hoping to make quick profits. By 1929, about 1.5 million Americans owned shares. Many were not experienced investors — just ordinary people caught up in the excitement.

Many bought shares ‘on the margin’ — borrowing money from banks and paying only 10% upfront. This worked while prices rose. If prices fell, investors would owe far more than their shares were worth.

Key Fact — Buying on the Margin

By 1929, $8.5 billion had been loaned for share purchases — more than the entire amount of money in circulation in the USA. The stock market was a giant bubble, inflated by borrowed money and blind optimism.

Hire Purchase and Easy Credit

The boom was fuelled by hire purchase (buying on credit). Millions of Americans bought cars, fridges, and radios on monthly instalments. This made people feel wealthy, but they were actually piling up debt. When the Crash came, many still owed money on goods they could no longer afford.

Overproduction

Factories produced far more goods than people could buy. Mass production churned out goods at record rates, but wages had not risen fast enough for most workers to keep up. By the late 1920s, warehouses were filling with unsold cars, fridges, radios, and clothing. Businesses cut production and laid off workers, reducing spending power even further.

Unequal Distribution of Wealth

1920s prosperity was shared very unevenly. The richest 5% of Americans received about 33% of all national income. Around 60% of families earned less than $2,000 per year — the minimum for a decent life. Too many people were too poor to buy consumer goods, so overproduction was inevitable.

Republican Laissez-Faire and Weak Banks

The Republican laissez-faire approach meant the government deliberately chose not to regulate banks. There were thousands of small, independent banks, many making risky loans to speculators and farmers. Banks even gambled with their customers’ deposits on the stock market. There was no federal deposit insurance, so if a bank failed, savers lost everything. The banking system was a house of cards.

Agricultural Problems

Farmers had struggled throughout the 1920s. Overproduction drove down crop prices, and many were deep in debt. When farmers could not repay loans, rural banks began to fail. This weakness spread to the wider economy.

International Trade Problems

American tariffs (like the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922) made foreign goods expensive, but other countries hit back with tariffs on American exports. This shrank overseas markets for American goods. European economies were also weak, further reducing demand.

The Events of October 1929

Confidence began to waver in September 1929 as experienced investors sold shares, sensing prices had risen too high. The situation collapsed rapidly:

‘Black Thursday’ (24 Oct): Panic selling began. Nearly 13 million shares were traded in one day. Leading bankers pooled money to buy shares and briefly steadied prices, but confidence was shattered.

‘Black Monday’ (28 Oct): Selling resumed harder. The bankers’ rescue failed. The market lost 13% in a single day.

‘Black Tuesday’ (29 Oct): The worst day. Over 16 million shares were dumped in panic. Prices collapsed. Margin investors were ruined — they owed more than their shares were now worth.

The weeks after: Prices kept falling. By mid-November the market had lost about $30 billion. There was no recovery — prices fell until 1932.

Immediate Consequences

The crash had devastating effects:

Investors Ruined

Millions who had invested their savings lost everything. Margin buyers were left with huge debts. Some wealthy investors were reduced to poverty overnight.

Banks Collapsed

Banks had lent huge sums to investors who could now not repay. By 1929–1932, over 5,000 banks collapsed. Ordinary savers lost everything because there was no government insurance. Panic spread as people rushed to withdraw cash from surviving banks, causing even more to fail.

Businesses Failed

With banks collapsing and credit drying up, businesses could not get loans. Consumer spending plummeted. Factories cut production, shops closed, companies went bankrupt. By 1933, industrial production had fallen nearly 50% from its 1929 level.

Unemployment Soared

Unemployment rose from about 1.5 million in 1929 to over 13 million by 1933 — roughly 25% of the workforce. With no welfare system, unemployed workers and their families faced destitution.

Key Fact — A Vicious Cycle

The crash created a downward spiral: share prices fell → investors lost money → banks failed → people lost savings → businesses closed → workers lost jobs → spending fell → more businesses closed. This vicious cycle plunged America into the Great Depression.

practice_questions.text: In what ways were the lives of Americans affected by the Wall Street Crash of 1929? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: The crash affected Americans at every level, creating a vicious downward spiral. Investors who had bought shares ‘on the margin’ were ruined — they owed more than their shares were worth. With $8.5 billion in margin loans outstanding, the losses were catastrophic. Over 5,000 banks failed between 1929 and 1932, wiping out the savings of ordinary Americans who had never invested in shares. With no federal deposit insurance, these savers lost everything. Businesses could not get credit, so they cut production and laid off workers. Industrial production fell nearly 50% by 1933. Unemployment rose from 1.5 million to over 13 million — 25% of the workforce. With no welfare system, unemployed families faced destitution. The psychological impact was also huge: the crash shattered the overconfidence of the 1920s boom. Herbert Hoover had promised ‘a chicken in every pot and two cars in every garage’ — instead, millions faced poverty. The crash did not affect everyone equally: the wealthy lost paper fortunes, but it was the poorest — those already struggling before the crash, like farmers and unskilled workers — who suffered most.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: Many investors lost everything because they had bought shares on the margin. Over 5,000 banks also collapsed, meaning ordinary savers lost their deposits. Unemployment rose to 13 million by 1933, and with no welfare system, families had no support.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: Banks collapsed after the crash. Over 5,000 banks failed and people lost all their savings because there was no government insurance.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: People lost their money and jobs after the crash.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the weaknesses of the 1920s economy lead to the Wall Street Crash? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: Several interconnected weaknesses combined to make the crash inevitable. Speculation was rampant — about 1.5 million Americans owned shares, and many bought on the margin with only 10% down. By 1929, $8.5 billion in margin loans inflated a massive bubble. This speculation was possible because Republican laissez-faire meant no regulation of banks or the stock market. Overproduction was another fundamental problem: factories churned out goods at record rates, but with the richest 5% taking 33% of all income and 60% of families earning below $2,000 a year, most Americans could not afford to buy them. Warehouses filled with unsold goods, profits fell, and share prices became disconnected from reality. Hire purchase masked the problem temporarily — 60% of cars and 80% of radios were bought on credit — but this just meant Americans were piling up debt. Agricultural problems added further weakness: farmers had struggled throughout the 1920s, and when they could not repay loans, rural banks failed. Tariffs like the Fordney-McCumber Tariff (1922) shrank overseas markets. These causes reinforced each other: overproduction led to falling profits, which made shares overvalued, which triggered panic selling when confidence finally broke.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: Speculation was a key weakness. Many Americans bought shares on the margin, paying only 10% upfront. By 1929, $8.5 billion had been loaned. Overproduction also weakened the economy — factories made more goods than people could buy because 60% of families earned less than $2,000 a year.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: Speculation meant people were buying shares with borrowed money, which created a bubble. When prices fell, investors owed more than their shares were worth.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The economy had problems like speculation and overproduction.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on causing the Wall Street Crash:

• speculation and buying on the margin
• overproduction and unequal wealth?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: Both were essential causes, and they were deeply connected. Speculation inflated the stock market bubble: about 1.5 million Americans owned shares, and many bought on the margin with only 10% down. By 1929, $8.5 billion in margin loans had been made — more than the total money in circulation. When experienced investors began selling in September 1929, margin buyers could not cover their debts, turning a dip into a catastrophic collapse. On Black Tuesday alone, over 16 million shares were dumped. However, the underlying reason share prices were unsustainable was overproduction and unequal wealth. Factories produced more goods than people could buy because 60% of families earned below $2,000 a year and the richest 5% took 33% of income. Warehouses filled with unsold goods, business profits fell, and share prices became disconnected from real value. Speculation was the immediate trigger — it turned weakness into crisis — but overproduction and inequality were the fundamental cause. Without them, the stock market would not have been so overvalued in the first place. The crash was inevitable because both sets of causes reinforced each other.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): Speculation inflated the bubble. Many Americans bought shares on the margin, paying only 10% upfront. By 1929, $8.5 billion had been loaned. When prices fell, investors were ruined — on Black Tuesday, 16 million shares were sold in panic.
Example (bullet 2): Overproduction meant factories made more goods than people could afford. The richest 5% received 33% of income, while 60% of families earned below $2,000. Unsold goods piled up and business profits fell.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: Speculation caused the crash because people borrowed money to buy shares. When prices fell, they could not pay back their loans.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The crash was caused by speculation and overproduction.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on the American economy in 1929:

• the events of Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
• the collapse of the banking system?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: Both were devastating, and the banking collapse was a direct consequence of the stock market crash. Black Thursday (24 October) saw nearly 13 million shares traded in one day as panic selling began. Leading bankers briefly steadied prices, but confidence was shattered. Black Tuesday (29 October) was the worst day — over 16 million shares were sold in panic, and margin investors were ruined. By mid-November, the market had lost about $30 billion. However, the banking collapse arguably had a deeper and longer-lasting impact on ordinary Americans. Banks had lent huge sums to investors and also gambled with customers’ deposits on the stock market. Over 5,000 banks failed between 1929 and 1932. With no federal deposit insurance, ordinary savers lost everything — not just investors, but families who had never bought a share. Panic bank runs caused even solvent banks to fail. Without functioning banks, businesses could not get loans, factories closed, and unemployment rose from 1.5 million to 13 million. The stock market crash was the trigger, but the banking collapse turned a financial crisis into the Great Depression that devastated the entire economy for years.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): Black Thursday and Black Tuesday wiped out investors. On Black Tuesday, over 16 million shares were sold and prices collapsed. By mid-November the market had lost $30 billion. Margin investors were ruined because they owed more than their shares were worth.
Example (bullet 2): Over 5,000 banks collapsed between 1929 and 1932. Ordinary savers lost all their money because there was no government deposit insurance. Without banks, businesses could not get loans and millions lost their jobs.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: On Black Tuesday over 16 million shares were sold and the market lost billions of dollars. Many investors were completely ruined.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The stock market crashed and banks failed, which caused the Depression.
0 marks: No relevant content.

Mass unemployment, Hoovervilles and the Dust Bowl — the devastating human impact of the worst economic crisis in US history.

before.content_html:
FDR’s Election in 1932

Franklin Delano Roosevelt (known as FDR) won the 1932 presidential election in a landslide, defeating the unpopular Herbert Hoover. He won 42 of 48 states and 57% of the popular vote. Americans were desperate for change. Roosevelt promised a ‘New Deal’ — a bold programme of government action to tackle the Depression.

Key Fact — Roosevelt’s Promise

In his acceptance speech, Roosevelt declared: ‘I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.’ At his inauguration on 4 March 1933, he said: ‘The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.’ He projected confidence and energy — a sharp contrast with Hoover’s perceived inaction.

Roosevelt’s Approach

FDR’s approach was very different from Hoover’s. He believed the federal government had a responsibility to help ordinary Americans in crisis. He surrounded himself with the ‘Brain Trust’ — a team of expert advisors from universities and business — to design his policies. His New Deal had three main aims, known as the ‘Three Rs’:

A key idea behind the New Deal was ‘priming the pump’. If the government spent money to create jobs, those workers would spend their wages in shops and businesses, which would then hire more workers. This would create a cycle of rising prosperity. In total, the New Deal cost $50.2 billion — the biggest government spending programme in world history at the time.

The First Hundred Days (March–June 1933)

Roosevelt acted fast. In his first 100 days, he pushed 15 major pieces of legislation through Congress. He also used ‘fireside chats’ — radio broadcasts to the nation — to explain his policies in simple, reassuring language. Around 60 million Americans listened.

The Emergency Banking Act (March 1933)

Roosevelt’s first act was to declare a ‘bank holiday’ — closing all banks for four days. Government inspectors checked every bank’s accounts. Only sound banks were allowed to reopen. This restored public confidence, and within weeks Americans were depositing money back into banks instead of hiding it at home.

The Alphabet Agencies

The New Deal created many new government agencies to tackle different parts of the Depression. These became known as the ‘alphabet agencies’ because of their abbreviations:

CCC — Civilian Conservation Corps (1933): Gave work to young unemployed men aged 18–25 in conservation projects — planting trees, building roads, and preventing soil erosion. Workers received $30 per month ($25 sent home to their families). By 1942, around 3 million young men had worked in the CCC. It planted over 3 billion trees. Around 200,000 African Americans served in the CCC, but women were banned entirely.

AAA — Agricultural Adjustment Administration (1933): Aimed to raise farm prices by paying farmers to produce less. Reducing supply pushed crop prices up. Farm income doubled between 1933 and 1939. However, critics argued it was wrong to destroy food when millions were hungry. It also hurt sharecroppers and tenant farmers who were evicted when landowners took land out of production.

TVA — Tennessee Valley Authority (1933): A huge government project to develop the Tennessee Valley, one of the poorest regions in America. The TVA built 21 dams to control flooding, generate cheap hydroelectric power, and improve navigation. It brought electricity to rural areas for the first time and transformed the region’s economy. The TVA is often seen as the most successful New Deal programme.

NRA — National Recovery Administration (1933): Set minimum wages, maximum working hours, and banned child labour. Businesses that signed up displayed the ‘Blue Eagle’ symbol. However, the Supreme Court declared the NRA unconstitutional in 1935 because it gave the federal government too much power over businesses.

FERA — Federal Emergency Relief Administration (1933): Gave $500 million in grants to states for direct relief — food, clothing, and shelter. This was the first time the federal government had given money directly to help the poor.

CWA — Civil Works Administration (1933): Run by Harry Hopkins, the CWA quickly created 4 million short-term jobs for unskilled workers during the harsh winter of 1933–34 — building roads, schools, and airports. It was replaced by the WPA in 1935.

PWA — Public Works Administration (1933): Run by Harold Ickes, the PWA focused on large-scale, skilled construction projects. It spent over $6 billion building 34,000 projects, including the Triborough Bridge in New York. The PWA used skilled workers; the CWA and WPA used mostly unskilled labour. This was a key distinction.

WPA — Works Progress Administration (1935): The largest New Deal agency. Run by Harry Hopkins, the WPA employed around 8.5 million people between 1935 and 1943. It built 650,000 miles of roads, 125,000 public buildings, and 8,000 parks. It also employed artists, writers, actors, and musicians. Critics mocked some WPA jobs as ‘boondoggles’ — pointless make-work like sweeping leaves, scaring pigeons from buildings, or putting on plays. The word came from old cowboy slang for a useless task.

The Second New Deal (1935–1937)

In 1935, Roosevelt launched a second wave of New Deal laws, focusing more on long-term reform and social welfare:

The Social Security Act (1935)

This was arguably the most important and lasting New Deal reform. It created:

  • A national pension system for Americans over 65
  • Unemployment insurance — for the first time, workers who lost their jobs received temporary financial support
  • Financial help for the disabled and for mothers with dependent children

The Social Security Act created America’s first welfare state. It established the principle that the federal government had a duty to care for its citizens — a revolutionary idea in the United States.

The Wagner Act (1935)

Also known as the National Labor Relations Act, this gave workers the legal right to join trade unions and bargain collectively with employers. It set up the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to protect workers’ rights. Union membership grew from 3.7 million in 1933 to 9 million by 1938.

Opposition to the New Deal

Despite its popularity, the New Deal faced strong opposition from several directions:

Opposition from the Right (Republicans and Big Business)

  • Republicans and business leaders accused Roosevelt of spending too much and creating dangerous federal power.
  • They called the New Deal ‘socialism’ or even ‘communism,’ saying it interfered with free enterprise and individual liberty.
  • The American Liberty League, funded by wealthy businessmen, campaigned against the New Deal.
  • Critics also attacked ‘boondoggles’ — claiming the government was paying people to do pointless jobs.

Opposition from the Left

  • Huey Long, the populist Senator from Louisiana, argued the New Deal did not go far enough. He proposed a ‘Share Our Wealth’ programme that would tax away the largest personal fortunes and share the money out, giving every American family a minimum income of $5,000 per year, a free education, and a car. Long attracted millions of followers before he was assassinated in 1935.
  • Father Charles Coughlin, a Catholic priest with a radio audience of 30–40 million, initially supported FDR but turned against him. He called the New Deal too friendly to bankers and not doing enough for ordinary people.
  • Dr Francis Townsend campaigned for a pension of $200 per month for all Americans over 60, funded by a national sales tax. His plan attracted 5 million supporters.

The Supreme Court

The Supreme Court was a major threat to the New Deal. In 1935, it declared the NRA unconstitutional, and in 1936 it struck down the AAA. Conservative judges argued that New Deal agencies gave the federal government powers that belonged to individual states. In 1937, Roosevelt tried to ‘pack’ the Court by adding up to six extra, sympathetic judges. This ‘court-packing’ plan was hugely controversial and was rejected by Congress.

Key Fact — The Court-Packing Crisis

Roosevelt’s attempt to add extra judges in 1937 was his biggest political mistake. Even his supporters saw it as an attempt to undermine the courts’ independence. The plan failed, but the Supreme Court then began ruling more favourably on New Deal laws — a shift called ‘the switch in time that saved nine.’

Despite all this opposition, Roosevelt won the 1936 election in a landslide, carrying all but 2 states. Only Maine and Vermont backed his opponent. This showed that ordinary Americans strongly supported his programmes, even if the rich and powerful did not.

Successes and Limitations of the New Deal

Jobs created: Millions were put back to work through the CCC, PWA, and WPA. Unemployment fell from 14 million (25%) in 1933 to 7 million (14%) by 1937.

Infrastructure: The New Deal built roads, bridges, dams, schools, hospitals, and airports that served America for decades. The TVA transformed an entire region.

Banking reform: The Emergency Banking Act and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) restored confidence in banks and protected savers.

Social Security: The Social Security Act (1935) created a lasting safety net — pensions, unemployment insurance, and disability support — that still exists today.

Workers’ rights: The Wagner Act strengthened trade unions and gave workers more bargaining power.

Hope and confidence: The New Deal restored hope. Roosevelt’s fireside chats and energetic leadership gave Americans confidence that their government cared.

Popular support: Roosevelt’s 1936 re-election (all but 2 states) proved the New Deal had wide public backing.

Did not end the Depression: Unemployment fell to 7 million by 1937, but when Roosevelt cut spending that year, the economy slipped back into recession (the ‘Roosevelt Recession’). Unemployment jumped back to 10 million. It was World War Two, not the New Deal, that finally ended the Depression.

African Americans: The New Deal did little for Black Americans. CCC camps were segregated. The AAA often helped white landowners at the expense of Black sharecroppers. Roosevelt refused to support anti-lynching legislation, fearing he would lose white Southern Democrats. Around 200,000 African Americans did benefit from the CCC, but discrimination was widespread.

Women: Most New Deal jobs were designed for men. Women were banned from the CCC entirely. Only around 8,000 women were enrolled in CCC-equivalent programmes, compared to 3 million men. Some NRA codes set lower wages for women than for men.

Huge government debt: The New Deal cost $50.2 billion in total — the biggest government scheme in world history. Critics said this was unsustainable.

Did not fix the economic system: American capitalism stayed the same. Wealth inequality persisted, and the root causes of the Depression were not fully addressed.

States’ Rights vs Federal Government

The New Deal permanently changed the relationship between the federal government and the American people. Before Roosevelt, most Americans expected state governments — not Washington — to handle welfare, jobs, and economic problems. The New Deal shifted power to the federal government on a scale never seen before. This was a revolutionary change. From this point on, Americans looked to the president and Congress to solve national crises. The debate over states’ rights versus federal power remains one of the biggest issues in American politics today.
before.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

Roosevelt’s New Deal was a turning point in American government. For the first time, the federal government took direct responsibility for citizens’ welfare — creating jobs, building infrastructure, and setting up a social safety net. It gave millions of Americans hope during the worst economic crisis in history. However, it did not end the Depression, and its benefits were uneven. The New Deal’s lasting legacy was a permanent shift of power from the states to the federal government — and the principle that government must protect its people from economic disaster.

Key Takeaways

  • FDR’s election (1932): Won 42 of 48 states. Promised a ‘New Deal’ based on Relief, Recovery, and Reform. His ‘Brain Trust’ of expert advisors designed the policies.
  • Alphabet agencies: CCC (3 million employed), TVA (21 dams), WPA (8.5 million employed). Total cost: $50.2 billion. Unemployment fell from 14 million to 7 million by 1937.
  • Limitations: Did not end the Depression (WWII did). African Americans and women benefited less. The ‘Roosevelt Recession’ (1937) saw unemployment jump back to 10 million after spending cuts.

The Social Security Act (1935) created America’s first welfare state — pensions, unemployment insurance, and disability support. However, the benefits were unevenly distributed. Women were banned entirely from the CCC, and only 8,000 women were enrolled in equivalent programmes compared to 3 million men. African Americans faced segregated CCC camps, and the AAA often helped white landowners at the expense of Black sharecroppers. Roosevelt refused to support anti-lynching legislation. The New Deal gave hope and created a lasting safety net, but it did not end the Depression — World War Two did that.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: The New Deal created millions of jobs through agencies like the CCC and WPA, cutting unemployment from 25% to 14% by 1937. The TVA built 21 dams, bringing electricity to the Tennessee Valley for the first time. However, African Americans benefited less — CCC camps were segregated and the AAA hurt Black sharecroppers.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: The CCC gave young men jobs planting trees and building roads, paying them $30 per month.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The New Deal created jobs for people.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the relationship between the federal government and the American people change because of the New Deal? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: Before Roosevelt, most Americans expected state governments — not Washington — to handle welfare and economic problems. Hoover’s ‘rugged individualism’ reflected this view. The New Deal completely changed this. Roosevelt used the federal government to spend $50.2 billion — the biggest government programme in world history — creating jobs, building infrastructure, and establishing the Social Security Act (1935), which gave Americans pensions, unemployment insurance, and disability support for the first time. The Emergency Banking Act and FDIC restored confidence in banks. The Wagner Act (1935) gave workers the legal right to join unions, increasing membership from 3.7 million to 9 million by 1938. However, this expansion of federal power was controversial. The Supreme Court struck down the NRA and AAA as unconstitutional. Republicans and the American Liberty League accused Roosevelt of socialism. His 1937 court-packing plan was rejected by Congress. Despite opposition, the principle that government must protect citizens from economic disaster became permanent. Americans now looked to Washington in times of crisis.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: The New Deal expanded the federal government’s role dramatically. The Social Security Act created pensions and unemployment insurance for the first time. Alphabet agencies like the WPA employed 8.5 million people directly. The Wagner Act strengthened trade unions. This shifted power from states to Washington on a scale never seen before.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: The New Deal meant the federal government started helping ordinary people directly, for example through the FERA which gave $500 million in grants to states.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The government started doing more to help people.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on the effects of the Depression in America:

• the actions of President Hoover
• the actions of President Roosevelt?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: Hoover’s actions made the Depression worse. His belief in ‘rugged individualism’ meant he refused direct relief. His Hawley-Smoot Tariff (1930) cut international trade as other countries retaliated. His late measures — $400 million in building projects and the RFC ($1,500 million in loans to banks) — helped businesses, not ordinary people. The Bonus Army attack in 1932 — soldiers using tear gas and tanks against 20,000 veterans — destroyed his reputation. Roosevelt’s actions had a far greater impact on relieving the Depression. His ‘Hundred Days’ produced 15 major laws. The Emergency Banking Act restored confidence. Alphabet agencies created millions of jobs: the CCC (3 million), WPA (8.5 million), and TVA (21 dams transforming the Tennessee Valley). The Social Security Act (1935) created pensions and unemployment insurance. Total spending was $50.2 billion. Unemployment fell from 14 million to 7 million by 1937. However, even Roosevelt did not end the Depression — the ‘Roosevelt Recession’ of 1937 saw unemployment rise back to 10 million when spending was cut. It was ultimately World War Two that ended the Depression. Roosevelt’s impact was greater because he took decisive action that directly helped millions, while Hoover’s inaction and mistakes deepened the crisis.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): Hoover believed in rugged individualism and refused direct relief. The RFC helped banks, not people. The Bonus Army attack showed he was out of touch.
Example (bullet 2): Roosevelt created the CCC, WPA, and TVA, putting millions back to work. The Social Security Act created a lasting safety net. He won the 1936 election carrying all but 2 states.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: Roosevelt helped more because he created jobs through agencies like the CCC and WPA.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Hoover did not do much but Roosevelt tried to help.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on American workers:

• the alphabet agencies (CCC, WPA, TVA)
• the Social Security Act and Wagner Act?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: The alphabet agencies had an immediate, visible impact. The CCC employed 3 million young men in conservation work, paying $30 per month. The WPA was the largest agency, employing 8.5 million people and building 650,000 miles of roads, 125,000 buildings, and 8,000 parks. The TVA built 21 dams, bringing electricity and flood control to one of America’s poorest regions. The PWA spent $6 billion on 34,000 projects. These agencies cut unemployment from 14 million to 7 million by 1937 and physically rebuilt America’s infrastructure. However, the Social Security Act and Wagner Act had a longer-lasting impact. The Social Security Act (1935) created America’s first welfare state — pensions for over-65s, unemployment insurance, and help for the disabled. This safety net still exists today. The Wagner Act gave workers the legal right to join unions and bargain collectively, increasing union membership from 3.7 million to 9 million by 1938. These laws permanently changed the relationship between government, workers, and employers. The alphabet agencies provided emergency relief, but the Social Security and Wagner Acts created structural changes that protected workers for decades to come.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): The CCC, WPA, and TVA directly employed millions and built lasting infrastructure. The TVA transformed the Tennessee Valley with 21 dams. Unemployment fell from 25% to 14% by 1937.
Example (bullet 2): The Social Security Act created pensions and unemployment insurance for the first time. The Wagner Act helped union membership grow from 3.7 million to 9 million.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: The WPA employed 8.5 million people and built roads, schools, and parks across America.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The New Deal agencies gave people jobs.
0 marks: No relevant content.

lessons.title: The Impact of World War Two

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the US economy was transformed by the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Upper band (3-4): Answers demonstrate knowledge and understanding. Students move from a simple demonstration of knowledge with extended reasoning supported by understanding of, for example, the ways in which events were problematic.
Example: One way was through war production. American factories switched from consumer goods to military equipment at astonishing speed. The Ford Willow Run plant went from making cars to building B-24 bombers — at its peak, one every 63 minutes. By 1945, American factories had produced 300,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, and 6,500 naval vessels. The government spent over $300 billion on the war effort, finally achieving full employment.
Another example: Another way was through Lend-Lease. Signed on 11 March 1941, the Lend-Lease Act supplied weapons, food, and equipment to the Allies totalling $50.1 billion. Britain received $31.4 billion and the Soviet Union $11.3 billion. Producing these goods employed millions of American workers and boosted the economy enormously.
Lower band (1-2): Answers demonstrate knowledge. Students demonstrate relevant knowledge about the issue(s) identified.
Example: Factories made weapons instead of consumer goods during the war.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways African Americans were affected by the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Upper band (3-4): Answers demonstrate knowledge and understanding. Students move from a simple demonstration of knowledge with extended reasoning supported by understanding of, for example, the ways in which events were problematic.
Example: One way was through new employment opportunities. After A. Philip Randolph threatened a March on Washington, Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 in June 1941 — the first federal order banning racial discrimination since Reconstruction. African Americans in defence industries rose from 3% (1942) to 8% (1945), and over one million Black workers gained factory jobs.
Another example: Another way was through military service. Over one million African Americans served in the US military, though the armed forces remained strictly segregated. Despite being given mainly non-combat roles, some units won distinction — the Tuskegee Airmen flew over 15,000 combat sorties and the 761st Tank Battalion earned a Presidential Unit Citation.
Lower band (1-2): Answers demonstrate knowledge. Students demonstrate relevant knowledge about the issue(s) identified.
Example: More African Americans got jobs in factories during the war.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the lives of African-Americans and women change during the Second World War? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: Both groups saw real progress but also continued inequality. For African Americans, Executive Order 8802 (1941) banned discrimination in defence industries for the first time, increasing Black workers from 3% to 8%. The Double V campaign politicised Black Americans by demanding victory over fascism abroad and racism at home. Over one million served in the military — the Tuskegee Airmen flew 15,000 combat sorties. However, the military remained segregated, Black workers earned half of white wages, and the 1943 Detroit race riot (34 dead) showed ongoing tensions. For women, the workforce grew from 12 million to 18 million — 37% of workers by 1944. They became welders, riveters, and pilots (WASPs). Over 300,000 served in military roles like the WAC and WAVES. But women earned only 65% of men’s pay, and after 1945, 4 million were pushed out to make way for returning soldiers, despite 75% wanting to keep their jobs. Both groups’ wartime experiences raised expectations that fuelled post-war demands for equality.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: Women entered the workforce in huge numbers — from 12 million to 18 million by 1945. ‘Rosie the Riveter’ became the symbol of women’s contribution. African Americans gained factory jobs through Executive Order 8802, and the Double V campaign raised awareness of racial injustice. However, both groups still faced inequality: women earned 65% of men’s wages, and the military remained segregated.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: Many women got jobs in factories during the war because 16 million men were in the armed forces. By 1944, women made up 37% of the workforce.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Women and African Americans got more jobs during the war.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: In what ways were the lives of Japanese Americans affected by the Second World War? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: Japanese Americans suffered one of the worst violations of civil liberties in American history. After Pearl Harbor (December 1941), anti-Japanese hysteria swept the country. In February 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorising the forced removal of all people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. About 120,000 Japanese Americans — two-thirds of them US citizens — were sent to ten remote internment camps. Families had only days to sell their homes and possessions, often for a fraction of their value, losing an estimated $400 million in property. Camps were surrounded by barbed wire and armed guards, and families lived in cramped barracks. No Japanese American was ever found guilty of spying or sabotage — the internment was driven by racial prejudice and wartime hysteria. Significantly, Japanese Americans in Hawaii were not interned, even though they made up a third of the population there, suggesting economic jealousy and racism were the real motives. The long-term impact was devastating: communities were broken apart and livelihoods destroyed. It was not until 1988 that President Reagan formally apologised and awarded $20,000 to each surviving internee.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.
Example: After Pearl Harbor, 120,000 Japanese Americans were interned in ten remote camps. Two-thirds were US citizens. They lost an estimated $400 million in property. The camps were surrounded by barbed wire. No Japanese American was ever convicted of spying.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of change. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning about one identified change.
Example: Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps after Pearl Harbor. About 120,000 people were affected.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of change(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Japanese Americans were treated badly during the war.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on America:

• the New Deal
• the Second World War?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: The New Deal had a huge impact on the role of government. Roosevelt’s alphabet agencies (CCC, WPA, TVA) employed millions and built lasting infrastructure. The Social Security Act (1935) created America’s first welfare state. The Wagner Act strengthened trade unions. Total spending was $50.2 billion, and unemployment fell from 14 million to 7 million by 1937. However, the New Deal did not end the Depression — the ‘Roosevelt Recession’ (1937) saw unemployment jump back to 10 million. The Second World War had an even greater impact. Government spending of $300 billion dwarfed the New Deal and finally achieved full employment. Unemployment fell from 14.6% to 1.2%. Average wages rose 44%. Personal savings jumped from $6.3 billion to $37 billion. By 1945, the USA held two-thirds of the world’s gold reserves and produced half its manufactured goods. The war also transformed society: 18 million women entered the workforce, Executive Order 8802 opened defence jobs to African Americans, and the GI Bill (1944) helped 8 million veterans attend college. Both had lasting impacts, but the war was the turning point — it ended the Depression, created the American superpower, and raised expectations for equality that shaped the next 30 years.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): The New Deal created the CCC (3 million employed), WPA (8.5 million), and Social Security Act. It established the principle that government should help citizens. But it did not end the Depression.
Example (bullet 2): WWII ended the Depression through $300 billion in spending. Women workers rose from 12 million to 18 million. The GI Bill helped 8 million veterans get education. The USA became the world’s dominant superpower.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: The Second World War ended the Depression because government spending of $300 billion created full employment.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Both the New Deal and the war helped America.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on the lives of African Americans:

• wartime employment opportunities
• military service during the Second World War?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: Both employment and military service transformed African American life, but in different ways. Wartime employment had the most immediate economic impact. A. Philip Randolph’s threatened March on Washington forced Roosevelt to issue Executive Order 8802 (June 1941) — the first federal order banning racial discrimination since Reconstruction. African Americans in defence industries rose from 3% to 8%, and over one million gained factory jobs. The Great Migration accelerated — 1.5 million Black Americans moved to northern and western cities for factory work between 1940 and 1945. However, Black workers were typically paid half of white wages, and the Detroit race riot (1943, 34 dead) showed the tensions new migration caused. Military service had a more symbolic and political impact. Over one million African Americans served, and units like the Tuskegee Airmen (15,000 combat sorties) and the 761st Tank Battalion proved Black soldiers’ ability. The Double V campaign — demanding victory over fascism abroad and racism at home — politicised millions. Service challenged racist claims of Black inferiority and gave veterans confidence to demand their rights. Both were important, but employment changes had a more direct, widespread economic effect on millions of families, while military service planted the seeds of the civil rights movement.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): Executive Order 8802 banned discrimination in defence industries. Over one million Black workers gained factory jobs. 1.5 million moved north during the Great Migration.
Example (bullet 2): The Tuskegee Airmen flew 15,000 missions. The Double V campaign demanded victory over racism at home as well as fascism abroad. Over one million served.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: Executive Order 8802 banned discrimination in defence industries, and African Americans in those jobs rose from 3% to 8%.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: African Americans got more jobs and served in the army during WWII.
0 marks: No relevant content.

before.description: Economic recovery through war production, Lend-Lease, and the changing experiences of African Americans and women on the home front.
The post-1945 economic boom, suburban growth, the baby boom, Rock ’n’ Roll and television — prosperity and its limits.
Cold War paranoia, loyalty tests and Senator McCarthy’s anti-communist witch-hunts — fear and its impact on American society.
Jim Crow segregation, Brown v. Board, the Montgomery Bus Boycott and Little Rock — the early struggle for racial equality.

lessons.title: Civil Rights: King, Malcolm X & Black Power

before.description: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides, the March on Washington, Malcolm X, Black Power and landmark legislation — the peak years of the civil rights movement.
The New Frontier and Great Society programmes — how two presidents tried to tackle poverty, education and health inequality.
Betty Friedan, NOW, the fight for equal pay, Roe v. Wade and the battle over the Equal Rights Amendment — women’s fight for equality.
An overview of change across the whole period — weighing progress against continuing inequality to judge how far America was a land of opportunity.
